source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication
finding: Entropy is the average code length floor for a source with known probabilities. The paper gives about 50 percent redundancy for English when structure up to about 8 letters is used.
numbers: Redundancy of ordinary English about 50 percent (context up to ~8 letters); found by several independent methods.
quote: The redundancy of ordinary English, not considering statistical structure over greater distances than about eight letters, is roughly 50%.
limits: Short-range statistical estimate only. Entropy needs a known distribution, not a model's own beliefs.
agent_relevance: Entropy means nothing until the agent has an explicit probability table, for example over candidate hypotheses.

source: Shannon (1948) A Mathematical Theory of Communication (noisy channel)
finding: Equivocation H(x|y) is the uncertainty left about x after seeing y. Information received is H(x) minus H(x|y). Capacity C is the maximum of that over input distributions.
numbers: Theorem 20 gives capacity for a band W with white thermal noise of power N.
limits: Assumes a known, stationary noise model. A checker with unknown noise has no known capacity.
agent_relevance: A probe's value is how much it is expected to cut uncertainty about the answer. A noisy check yields less than one bit per query.

source: Shannon (1951) Prediction and Entropy of Printed English
finding: Human prediction experiments bound the entropy of literary English. Long-range structure up to 100 letters brings it to about one bit per letter.
numbers: Bounds on entropy per letter for context N=1..15 and 100: upper 4.03, 3.42, 3.0, 2.6, 2.7, 2.2, 2.8, 1.8, 1.9, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.1, 1.7, 2.1, then 1.3 at N=100; lower 3.19, 2.50, 2.1, 1.7, 1.7, 1.3, 1.8, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.3, 1.3, 1.2, 0.9, 1.2, then 0.6 at N=100. Redundancy roughly 75 percent. Single-letter entropy 4.14 bits vs 4.7 for uniform 26 letters.
quote: the long range statistical effects (up to 100 letters) reduce the entropy to something of the order of one bit per letter
limits: Few subjects and one text type. Shannon notes considerable sampling error. The lower bound is proved only for an ideal predictor and human guessers are not ideal.
agent_relevance: Estimated entropy falls as the predictor conditions on more context. Report any uncertainty number together with what it conditions on.

source: Shannon (1951) Prediction and Entropy of Printed English (comparison with 1948)
finding: Between the two papers the redundancy estimate for English rose from about 50 to about 75 percent as the allowed context grew from 8 to 100 letters.
numbers: 50 percent (1948, ~8 letters) vs 75 percent (1951, 100 letters).
limits: My comparison of two papers I read. A direct modern replication of the guessing experiment was not found in the sources I opened; the later Cover and King (1978) estimate was not opened and is not cited here.
agent_relevance: A prior-only entropy overstates uncertainty once evidence is in. Recompute after each answer.

source: Crupi, Nelson, Meder, Cevolani, Tentori (2018) Generalized information theory meets human cognition
finding: Shannon entropy is one member of a family (Hartley, quadratic, Tsallis, Renyi) unified in the Sharma-Mittal framework. Which member best fits human information search is treated as open.
numbers: No figures in the abstract; paper analyses published behavioural data.
limits: Abstract only, read through a Europe PMC record. Full text not opened.
agent_relevance: The choice of uncertainty measure is a design choice. Compare several on held-out outcomes.

source: Nelson (2005) Finding useful questions: Bayesian diagnosticity, probability, impact, and information gain
finding: Models of the selection task, categorisation and diagnosis experiments do not separate information gain, probability gain and impact. Bayesian diagnosticity is normatively flawed and a new experiment contradicts it.
numbers: No counts in abstract.
quote: Bayesian diagnosticity is normatively flawed and empirically unjustified.
limits: Abstract only. Does not separate information gain from probability gain.
agent_relevance: Do not pick probes by likelihood ratio alone. Use expected information gain or expected error reduction.

source: Nelson, McKenzie, Cottrell, Sejnowski (2010) Experience matters: information acquisition optimizes probability gain
finding: Three experiments designed by computer optimisation to discriminate four theories. With experience-based learning of probabilities, probability gain explained human search better than information gain, KL distance, impact or the probability-of-certainty heuristic.
numbers: Three experiments; sample sizes not in abstract. Behaviour differed when probabilities were given as verbal summary statistics instead of experience (Experiments 1 and 2). Preference for probability gain robust in Experiment 3.
quote: found that probability gain explained subjects' information search better than the other statistical theories
limits: Abstract only. Human result, not an LLM result.
agent_relevance: A rival to entropy: choose the probe that most cuts expected error. The two scores can disagree. Test both.

source: Coenen, Nelson, Gureckis (2019) Asking the right questions about the psychology of human inquiry: nine open challenges
finding: Critical review: the Optimal Experiment Design hypothesis is not yet a good theory of human inquiry, and nine questions stay open.
numbers: Nine open questions; no effect sizes in abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Human behaviour does not prove entropy-optimal probing is what good thinkers do. Our own measurements decide (G7).

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty: linguistic invariances for uncertainty estimation in NLG
finding: Token-level entropy mixes up form and meaning. Clustering sampled answers by two-way entailment and taking entropy over meaning classes (semantic entropy) predicts answer correctness better.
numbers: AUROC for predicting correctness: semantic entropy 0.77 (CoQA) and 0.83 (TriviaQA); count of distinct answers 0.66 and 0.79. Mean distinct meanings, correct vs incorrect: 1.27 vs 1.77 (CoQA), 1.89 vs 3.89 (TriviaQA). Advantage grows with model size.
quote: a model which is uncertain about whether to generate "France's capital is Paris" or "Paris is France's capital" is not uncertain in any important sense
limits: Needs several samples plus an entailment model. AUROC is moderate. Tested on question answering, not multi-step reasoning.
agent_relevance: Compute uncertainty over answer classes counted in code, not over token strings. Fits S7 and G5.

source: Kuhn et al. (2023) Semantic Uncertainty: sampling trade-off
finding: Number of samples and sampling temperature interact: more diversity helps detect uncertainty but lowers sample accuracy, so the two effects compete.
numbers: Plots only; I did not extract the peak values.
quote: we find that these two effects compete
limits: Read from text around the figures, not from a table.
agent_relevance: Sample count and temperature are parameters to tune on our tasks.

source: Farquhar, Kossen, Kuhn, Gal (2024) Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy (Nature)
finding: Extends semantic entropy to detect confabulations, meaning arbitrary wrong generations, across datasets and tasks without task-specific data.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
quote: computing uncertainty at the level of meaning rather than specific sequences of words
limits: Abstract only. By design it targets arbitrary errors; a consistent wrong answer has low entropy.
agent_relevance: Low entropy is not proof of correctness. Samples from one model are correlated (G4).

source: Kossen et al. (2024) Semantic Entropy Probes
finding: Semantic entropy costs 5 to 10 times more compute. A linear probe on hidden states of a single generation predicts it, and generalises better out of distribution than probes trained on correctness labels.
numbers: Probe AUROC 0.7 to 0.95 by task and layer. SEP minus accuracy-probe AUROC in-distribution: Mistral-7B +2.8 (se 1.4), Phi-3 +2.1 (0.8), Llama-2-7B -0.5 (2.6), Llama-2-70B +1.3 (0.7); long form Llama-2-70B -1.9 (7.5), Llama-3-70B -2.0 (2.1).
quote: SEPs can capture semantic entropy even before generation
limits: Needs open weights. Most in-distribution differences are within about one standard error. Some high AUROC on BioASQ comes from spotting yes/no questions.
agent_relevance: Not usable on a hosted model without hidden states. Use sampled answer-class entropy there.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false questions when formatted well; calibration improves with size and few-shot examples. P(IK), a trained estimate of whether the model knows, only partly generalises and is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: Models up to 52B. RLHF policies are miscalibrated at temperature 1; calibration curves shown at T=2.5 as the fix.
quote: Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks.
limits: Calibration depends on prompt format; replacing an option with None of the above harms it; RLHF harms it. Older models.
agent_relevance: Model probabilities are trustworthy only in some formats. Use frequencies counted in code and test calibration on our tasks.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking
finding: A planning tree simulates answers to candidate questions and scores each question by expected information gain over a list of possibilities. Tested on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Average success-rate gain over direct prompting 38.1 percent across LLMs (46.6 for Llama3-70B). Beats CoT-SC by 33.8 and Reflexion by 29.9; Original-ToT by 28.3 and Adapted-ToT by 12.4. GPT-4: 97.0 percent on the diagnosis set, troubleshooting 43.7 to 67.3 percent, MedDG 88.0 percent.
quote: UoT achieves an average performance improvement of 38.1% in the rate of successful task completion
limits: Closed-set: the possibilities are given. Authors list open-set as a limit. Gains mix planning and entropy, so entropy alone is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S7: score probes by expected information gain over an explicit hypothesis list.

source: Hu et al. (2024) UoT efficiency and reward variants
finding: Pruned UoT is less effective than full UoT but still beats ToT at comparable token use. Reward-variant spreads on GPT-3.5 are small except one variant that is worse on the first dataset.
limits: Column labels were lost in text extraction, so which dataset each number belongs to is uncertain. GPT-3.5 only.
agent_relevance: Having an explicit expected-gain score matters more than its exact form.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design (ICLR 2026)
finding: Choosing each question by expected information gain (EIG) from the LLM's predictive distribution roughly doubles 20 Questions success over prompting.
numbers: Mean +37.4 percentage points over direct prompting; success more than doubles in over half of setups and never decreases. Animals GPT-4o: Prompt-Only 45, CoT 62, Split 83, Entropy 88, BED-LLM 93. Celebrities Mistral-Large: 19 vs 91. Things Llama-3.1-8B: 10 vs 26. 100 targets per set; se about 3 to 5 points.
quote: predictive entropy is not a suitable surrogate for EIG
limits: Small models stay low (26 percent on Things). The authors say their Prompt-Only baseline is much stronger than earlier reports, so gains depend on the baseline.
agent_relevance: Strongest recent support for S7: use EIG, not raw entropy of the answer.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM ablations
finding: Replacing EIG with plain predictive entropy costs several points. Asking the LLM to pick the most informative question is a cheap middle option. Skipping hypothesis filtering hurts most.
numbers: Animals GPT-4o: BED-LLM 93, Entropy 88, Implicit Max 70, Data-Estimation 70, ICL Beliefs 25. Celebrities Qwen2.5-72B: BED-LLM 84, Entropy 59, Implicit 39. Film example: an ice-cream question has high predictive entropy but EIG = 0.
quote: Entropy provides the strongest alternative, with performance slightly better than Split.
limits: Gap between EIG and entropy varies from 5 to 25 points by model and set. Same benchmark family throughout.
agent_relevance: Raw entropy rewards irrelevant questions. Keep hypotheses consistent with past answers in code, then score by EIG.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Reasoning over candidate solutions and picking questions by EIG beats reasoning only in question space, in 20 Questions and code-requirement elicitation.
numbers: 20 Questions rankings averaged over 15 animals, 5 run seeds and 25 evaluation seeds: EIG-uniform ranks first, above implicit and implicit-ToT strategies. No percentages extracted. EIG strategies need more LLM calls than baselines.
quote: Shifting the reasoning load from question space to direct reasoning about solutions results in improved efficacy of the selected questions
limits: Only rankings were read. BED-LLM states its own baselines reach far higher results than reported here. Stopping and ambiguity detection are left open.
agent_relevance: List hypotheses first, then score probes against them.

source: Handa et al. (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN picks questions by Bayesian optimal experimental design and uses the LLM for features and wording. In a user study it beat LM-only and BOED-only elicitation.
numbers: Metric: time-integrated delta accuracy. About 44 users in at least one arm. Exact values not extracted.
quote: OPEN outperforms existing language-model-based and BOED-based methods for preference elicitation
limits: Pairwise queries in content recommendation, fixed feature space, one closed-source LM. Part of the gain came from OPEN's prediction method, not the question rule.
agent_relevance: Code does the information bookkeeping, the model does language. Same split as our schema.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman, Andreas (2023) Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models (GATE)
finding: Letting the LM ask open-ended questions or generate edge cases elicited more informative answers than user-written prompts or labels in preregistered studies.
numbers: Three domains: email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning. No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Questions were not scored by information gain.
agent_relevance: Free-form questioning is a cheap baseline entropy must beat at equal tokens.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: asking questions in Battleship
finding: Sampling questions from an LLM, translating them to programs and keeping the highest-EIG one reaches human-level questions. LLM-only baselines do not use the board state well.
numbers: Human data from Rothe et al. (2017): N=40, 605 question-board pairs, 18 boards. Grammar questions mean EIG 0.36 bits; CodeLlama and GPT-4 baselines 0.65 to 0.66. With k=5 samples near human mean; k=10 above human mean (p<0.001 CodeLlama, p=0.01 GPT-4); k=20 and 50 still below the best human questions. GPT-4V with visual board no better than no board.
quote: LLM-only baselines struggle to ground questions in the board state
limits: One small-board task with a symbolic scorer; needs a world model to compute EIG.
agent_relevance: Best-of-k probes with an explicit EIG scorer in code beats a single sampled probe.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LIPS: question validity
finding: Many LLM-written questions fail to translate to valid programs.
numbers: Translation success about 75 percent (CodeLlama) and 88 percent (GPT-4). Table text was partly garbled, so other validity rates are not cited.
limits: Approximate; table extraction was messy.
agent_relevance: Filter generated probes by running them and require EIG above zero.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2023) and Zhang et al. (2024), as cited in BED-LLM
finding: BED-LLM cites these as showing LLMs write coherent single questions but adapt poorly to earlier answers in multi-turn guessing games.
numbers: No numbers in the citing text.
quote: they typically struggle to appropriately tailor their questions to previously gathered responses
limits: Second-hand: I read BED-LLM's citation, not the cited papers.
agent_relevance: Re-score probes after every answer, in code.

source: Kuhn 2023 on limits of entropy as an error signal
finding: With best AUROC of 0.77 to 0.83, entropy misranks a real share of cases. By definition a model that always gives the same wrong answer has low semantic entropy.
numbers: AUROC 0.77 (CoQA) and 0.83 (TriviaQA).
limits: The confident-wrong point is my inference from the definition; the paper gives no count of such cases.
agent_relevance: Entropy finds unsure cases only. Pair it with an external check (G3).

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM on belief quality
finding: Raw in-context beliefs from the LLM are often incoherent. Filtering the hypothesis set against past answers is the largest single contributor.
numbers: ICL Beliefs (no filtering) vs BED-LLM: Animals GPT-4o 25 vs 93; GPT-4o-mini 18 vs 88.
limits: Filtering assumes noise-free answers, true of 20 Questions but not of a noisy checker.
agent_relevance: Maintain the hypothesis list in code. With a noisy checker, update weights instead of deleting.

source: Nelson 2005, Nelson 2010 and Crupi 2018 taken together
finding: Past human data could not tell information gain from probability gain. Optimised experiments favour probability gain under experience learning. Crupi puts both inside one entropy family.
numbers: Not numerical.
limits: Synthesis of three abstracts, not of full texts.
agent_relevance: Run both scores on our S7 and keep the one that predicts held-out success.
